evaluation.positioning_hook: A lonely nine-year-old discovers a magical seahorse in her coastal town, then leads a child protest to save it when an oil tycoon turns the creature into a profit machine.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has clear family appeal: a child bonds with a magical sea creature, and the emotional engine is easy to grasp. The market is narrower than a broad four-quadrant fantasy because the script leans heavily on a specific coastal, anti-corporate fable rather than a mainstream adventure engine.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and cleanly: Karissa finds Star, the seahorse becomes a secret family pet, and Thompson’s attempt to seize it creates the central conflict. The script keeps the premise legible through the town meeting, the seizure, and the sea park protest.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Karissa has a strong emotional center, and Boone’s guilt-ridden father energy gives the story a workable adult counterweight. The supporting adults are functional but mostly archetypal, with Thompson carrying the clearest personality.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The seahorse concept is unusual and the script commits to it with full sincerity, including the later reveal of a giant father seahorse and the oil-slick cleanup. The execution is more fable-like than subversive, but the creature design and environmental allegory give it a distinct lane.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story moves in clean, readable beats from discovery to seizure to protest to catastrophe, and the escalation is easy to follow. Some middle passages play as repeated variations on the same emotional idea—kids love seahorses, adults want control—before the final disaster kicks in.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a child’s secret pet becoming a public environmental and political flashpoint feels fresh and immediately understandable. The giant seahorse rescue at the end gives the premise a mythic payoff that is memorable without becoming opaque.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The coastal town, oil platform, and community-festival setting give the script a usable social texture, especially in the ensemble picnic and town protest scenes. The world is still primarily a container for the central fable rather than a deeply layered ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a clear storybook register: earnest, playful, and lightly satirical around corporate greed. The tone is consistent from the children’s club scenes through the sea park climax, which helps the material feel ownable.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are thematic seeds around divorce, belonging, stewardship, and the way institutions claim wonder for profit. But the script largely states its values directly, so the depth is present more as theme than as layered subtext.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The children’s club, the parent group, and the Thompson/Ross dynamic create recurring relationship combinations that generate scenes beyond the lead-child bond. Karissa/Willis, Karissa/Jim, Boone/Marla, and Thompson/Ross all have enough friction to keep the ensemble active.

lead_characters.name: Karissa Boone
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 9 years old, white, coastal New England child.
lead_characters.hook: A withdrawn, emotionally guarded little girl who speaks sparingly but feels everything intensely. Karissa is the story’s moral center: she’s lonely enough to bond with a magical creature, brave enough to challenge adults, and wounded enough that the seahorse becomes a stand-in for the family stability she can’t control.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a young performance like Brooklynn Prince in The Florida Project — a child role that lives on emotional truth, stillness, and sudden conviction. It gives a young actor the chance to carry the movie’s heart and to play innocence, grief, and leadership in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Drew Boone
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, white, oceanologist and divorced father.
lead_characters.hook: A scraggly, intelligent, emotionally compromised scientist who wants to do right by his daughter but keeps folding under pressure from the world and from himself. Drew is part dad, part believer, part coward, and the script uses that contradiction to make him sympathetic without making him heroic too early.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Mark Ruffalo in Spotlight or Michael Keaton in Birdman a chance to play intelligence, fragility, and self-reproach in one package. It offers a character actor a warm, wounded father role with enough comic awkwardness and moral pressure to register.

lead_characters.name: Martin Thompson
lead_characters.hook: A polished, smug oil-company operator who treats greed as civic virtue and never stops smiling while he takes what he wants. Thompson is the script’s clearest antagonist because he’s not chaotic; he’s bureaucratic, performative, and perfectly comfortable weaponizing law, media, and public relations.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of a Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad-style transformation role, but in reverse: a man whose charm is the mask and whose entitlement is the engine. It gives an actor a big, scene-stealing villain with comic vanity, public-facing polish, and real menace.

lead_characters.name: Ken Crimson
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 30s-40s, white, deputy sheriff and father.
lead_characters.hook: A rule-bound local cop whose authority is constantly undercut by his son’s conscience and by Thompson’s leverage. Crimson is interesting because he’s not corrupt in a cartoon way; he’s compromised, embarrassed, and trying to keep his family and his badge intact at the same time.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded authority role that lets an actor play the conflicted father energy of Kyle Chandler in Friday Night Lights. It offers a clean emotional turn from stern civic figure to a man whose son forces him to choose what kind of adult he is.

lead_characters.name: Willis Rosenberg
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 9 years old, white, brainy child.
lead_characters.hook: A precocious, socially precise kid whose awkward formality makes him the perfect counterpoint to Karissa’s silence. Willis is the script’s smartest child voice, and his dry, almost miniature-adult manner gives him real comic and emotional charm.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a young actor the scene-stealing precision of a young Jacob Tremblay or a child version of Michael Cera’s deadpan rhythm. It offers verbal comedy, awkward sincerity, and a sweet romantic-adjacent crush without losing innocence.

lead_characters.name: Jim Crimson
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 10 years old, white, deputy sheriff’s son.
lead_characters.hook: A swaggering, impulsive kid who starts as a bully and becomes one of the story’s most emotionally legible converts. Jim’s arc is useful because he gives the movie a kid who can be loud, physical, and wrong before becoming a believer in the seahorses’ cause.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets a young actor play the combustible energy of a young Noah Jupe in Honey Boy or a kid-version of a classic troublemaker. It has physicality, attitude, and a real turn toward vulnerability when he loses Striker.

lead_characters.name: Marla Boone
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 50s, white, Drew’s mother and Karissa’s grandmother.
lead_characters.hook: A warm, intuitive matriarch who sees the emotional weather before anyone else does. Marla functions as the script’s quiet wisdom figure, but she also has enough wit and authority to keep the household from becoming sentimental mush.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the grounded grace of Frances McDormand in a family setting or Margo Martindale in a prestige ensemble. It offers maternal authority, comic timing, and the chance to be the emotional ballast of the movie.

lead_characters.name: Alan Ross
lead_characters.hook: Thompson’s obedient, slightly owlish right hand, the kind of man who translates bad ideas into paperwork. Ross is a useful pressure valve because he’s not the villain’s equal, but he’s close enough to reveal how the machine works.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives a character actor the dry, subordinate energy of a Steve Buscemi or Paul Giamatti sidekick function. It’s a sharp supporting part with comic compliance and just enough moral cowardice to be memorable.

lead_characters.name: Dan Tanna
lead_characters.hook: A friendly, lightly comic neighborhood dad who helps make the town ensemble feel lived-in. He’s not a plot engine, but he gives the community scenes warmth and a sense that these families actually know one another.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a solid ensemble dad role in the lane of a character actor like Pat Healy or Paul Sparks in a lighter register. It gives an actor a few clean comic beats and the chance to make the town feel real.

lead_characters.name: Deneise Lamont
lead_characters.hook: A flirtatious, socially sharp single mother who brings adult friction and a little comic heat to the picnic scenes. Deneise is useful because she keeps the town from feeling too wholesome and gives the adult ensemble some romantic static.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play the lively, slightly dangerous energy of a Melanie Lynskey-type supporting turn. It offers comic vanity, flirtation, and a real personality in a small footprint.

lead_characters.name: Grace Crimson
lead_characters.hook: A practical, no-nonsense spouse who sees through the men around her faster than they expect. Grace gives the Crimson household a grounded adult intelligence and helps keep Ken from becoming a one-note authority figure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the crisp domestic authority of Connie Britton in a family drama. It’s a sharp supporting wife role with enough skepticism and backbone to matter.

lead_characters.name: Teresa Tanna
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 9 years old, white, socially polished child.
lead_characters.hook: A prim, slightly snooty kid who wants to be taken seriously and mostly succeeds by sheer confidence. Teresa is a good foil for Karissa because she gives the children’s group a social hierarchy and a comic sense of status games.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a fun child supporting role in the lane of a young scene-stealer who can play superiority without losing charm. It gives a young actor crisp dialogue and a distinct social posture.

lead_characters.name: Tasha Lamont
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 9 years old, white, imitative child.
lead_characters.hook: A copycat little girl who follows the social current around her and helps widen the children’s club into a real group. Tasha is less defined than Karissa or Willis, but she adds texture and a sense of peer dynamics.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but useful child role that gives a young actor a chance to play reaction, imitation, and group energy. It’s the kind of part that helps populate the world without demanding a heavy lift.

casting_characteristics: one child lead carrying the emotional spine
multiple child supporting roles with distinct personalities
one antagonist with strong comic-villain presence

technical.vfx_details: Creature work for multiple seahorses, a 250-foot father seahorse, tidal-wave destruction, and the final oil-whirlpool cleanup sequence.
technical.sfx_needs: Water effects, flooding, practical destruction of the sea park, and oil-spill simulation.

rights_flags.detail: ATOIL / Atlantic Oil is a fictionalized corporate brand used prominently throughout.
CNN is named in the protest coverage scene.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: family-friendly theatrical or streaming-original with broad parental co-viewing appeal.

budget.note: The contemporary coastal setting is manageable, but the offshore platform, sea park build, tidal-wave destruction, and multiple creature effects will push this above a simple contained family feature.

casting.note: The movie depends on a child lead who can carry sincerity, defiance, and grief, plus a villain with comic bluster and real authority. The supporting child ensemble also needs distinct, readable personalities.

development.note: The script’s fable logic is clear, but the final act’s giant seahorse reveal and environmental-catastrophe scale will be a key buyer conversation about tone and audience expectation.

comp_set.title: Free Willy
comp_set.why_it_comps: A child bonds with a captive sea creature and the emotional engine is rescue, freedom, and public spectacle.

comp_set.title: The Water Horse
comp_set.why_it_comps: A coastal child fantasy built around a secret creature, family attachment, and a gentle mythic register.

comp_set.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
comp_set.why_it_comps: The core pleasure is a child protecting a wondrous being from adult systems that want to study and control it.

comp_set.title: The NeverEnding Story
comp_set.why_it_comps: The script leans into earnest fantasy, child wonder, and a creature-driven emotional quest.

audience_target.primary_audience: Families and adults who respond to heartfelt creature stories, especially parents and kids looking for an emotional, PG-friendly fantasy with a clear moral center.
audience_target.demographics: Kids 7-14, parents 30-49, family co-viewing, broad middle-American and coastal family audience.

budget_tier.note: Creature effects, water work, a sea park build, and a large-scale tidal climax put this in mid-budget family fantasy territory.

types_of_buyers: indie distributor seeking crossover family title
producer with creature-effects and water-production experience
lane_fit.detail: The script sits naturally in the lane of earnest, high-concept family fantasy with a civic message. It has enough wonder for kids, enough sentiment for parents, and enough spectacle to justify a real release plan.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a complete emotional arc; the seahorse family is memorable, but there is no clear sequel or spinoff vector that rises above one-off story value.

strengths.dimension_or_area: A child-protects-creature hook that lands fast.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project an immediately legible emotional engine that buyers can pitch in one sentence and parents can understand instantly. It is especially attractive to family buyers and streamers looking for a clean, high-concept hook with heart.
strengths.evidence: Karissa discovers Star on the beach, names him, brings him home, and later leads the protest to save him from Thompson.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The antagonist is a clean corporate villain.
strengths.what_it_means: Thompson gives the movie a strong, marketable human antagonist whose greed is easy to read and easy to hate. That clarity helps the film play to younger audiences while still giving adults a recognizable real-world pressure point.
strengths.evidence: Thompson seizes the seahorses, builds Seahorse Cove, and uses law and media to frame the children as the problem.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The children’s ensemble has real play value.
strengths.what_it_means: The Karissa/Willis/Jim/Teresa/Tasha group creates multiple kid-facing relationship combinations, which broadens the movie beyond a single pet story. That makes the material more attractive to family buyers who want repeatable charm and group dynamics.
strengths.evidence: The seahorse club oath, the naming of each seahorse, and the protest chain at the park entrance all give the ensemble a shared identity.

strengths.what_it_means: The tidal-wave destruction, giant father seahorse reveal, and oil-whirlpool cleanup give the movie a real third-act event movie finish. That helps the script justify a larger production conversation than a simple talking-creature family piece.
strengths.evidence: The sea park floods, Karissa nearly drowns, and Father appears to purge the oil slick with the family seahorses.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone is earnest and easy to brand.
strengths.what_it_means: The script knows what it is: a sincere, fable-like family fantasy with environmental stakes and a clear moral center. That kind of tonal consistency is valuable because it makes the project easier to position to parents, streamers, and family divisions.
strengths.evidence: The script repeatedly returns to Karissa’s promise, the “Keepsies” motif, and Marla’s gentle wisdom about belief and stewardship.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, pitchable family fantasy with a strong child-creature bond, a hateable corporate villain, and a finale that scales from intimate emotion to real spectacle. The combination of a simple hook, ensemble kid appeal, and mid-budget creature/water set pieces makes it a credible target for a streamer or studio family division looking for an original title with heart.

items.area: The final-act scale pushes the budget conversation.
items.detail: The sea park build, tidal-wave destruction, underwater rescue, giant father seahorse, and oil-whirlpool cleanup are all expensive asks in the same climax. That makes the movie materially bigger than its early family-fable setup suggests, and buyers will notice the tier pressure immediately.

items.area: Thompson is broad before he is dangerous.
items.detail: He reads as a cartoonish corporate bully in the festival and office scenes, with a lot of public bluster and very little interiority. That makes him easy to hate, but it also narrows the range of actors and can flatten the middle of the movie if the performance doesn’t carry him.

items.area: The middle repeats the same emotional beat.
items.detail: A lot of the center section cycles through variations of kids bonding with seahorses, adults reacting, and Thompson looming in the background. The material is pleasant, but the buyer will see that the story’s engine is strongest at the discovery, seizure, protest, and climax points rather than in the stretch between them.

items.area: The creature logic is intentionally fable-like.
items.detail: The seahorses appear, multiply, and behave according to story need rather than hard rules, which is fine for a family fantasy but still a buyer consideration. The script is asking the audience to accept mythic logic, not procedural logic, and that defines the lane pretty sharply.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is economic, not conceptual: it starts like a modest family fantasy and ends like a water-heavy creature spectacle with a large destruction sequence. The other buyer conversation is tonal—Thompson is a useful villain, but he’s broad enough that the movie will depend on performance and packaging to keep him from feeling one-note.
